#8315. Kayaking 3,700km Around Britain

Dominic Gribbin, 61, is more than five months into his attempt to circumnavigate mainland Great Britain by sea kayak. But relentless weather delays and mounting costs have made the journey even more challenging than anticipated.

Gribbin launched his expedition from Crinan Harbour in Argyll, Scotland, on June 2. Paddling clockwise, he has covered 2,584km. From Crinan, he continued up the west coast of Scotland and around Cape Wrath and Duncansby Head before heading south along the eastern and southern coasts. His latest reported landing point is Cliff End, near Hastings, Sussex.

The journey has not gone according to plan. Persistent Atlantic weather systems have cost him weeks of paddling time, while the financial demands of keeping the expedition moving have forced him to return to freelance television camerawork so he and his wife, Nicola, can keep it running.

While he paddles, she follows him in their motor home, offering shore support. He now hopes to complete the circle at Crinan in the spring of 2027. ExplorersWeb caught up with him to find out more about the journey. This interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.

How do you approach the daily distances on a journey like this?

Given that circumnavigating the British mainland is at least 3,700km, I have aimed to do at least 40km per day. My longest day so far has been 64km. However, weather, tides and daylight length, particularly in autumn and winter, often curtail one’s best-laid plans. Some days have been necessarily shorter, forcing me to make an earlier-than-envisaged retreat to shore.

But this is very much a journey, not a race, so we will continue into the spring of 2027. It’s an incredible opportunity to explore every nook and cranny of the GB coastline.

How much has the weather affected your progress?

Roughly 85% of delays have been due to poor weather, 5% to Ministry of Defense firing range timetable restrictions, and 10% to the need for very specific tidal windows to navigate particular sections safely and efficiently. I have never had a delay due to fatigue or the need for a break from the sheer physical nature of this endurance challenge. I have used days when I have inevitably been “weathered-off” to recoup my energy reserves.

For most of the trip, it has been extremely rare to have more than four days of consistently good paddling weather. Setting off from Crinan on June 2 meant we did not enjoy the heat wave experienced in southern Britain. Instead, we lost at least six weeks to poor weather. Constant Atlantic westerly and northwesterly fronts brought wind, rain, and high seas that seemed to permanently batter northwest and northern Scotland throughout June, July, and even into early August. It was one of the great untalked-about weather phenomena of summer 2026. It wasn’t all heat waves…at least not in Scotland!

Are you camping or sleeping in the motorhome?

Northwest Scotland and its wild, deeply indented coastline often made road access to the sea impossible. Early on, we accepted that there would be long stretches when Nicola would not see me for over 24 hours. She was often doing double the mileage I was doing and negotiating some very hairy driving conditions on roads way off the beaten track. That resulted in many planned and unplanned wild camps along the coast.

By the time we reached the north coast of Scotland, road access had improved dramatically, and Nicola and I were generally able to coordinate to meet at the end of each day. This has proved an invaluable motivator, especially when the going gets tough. Our little motorhome has been a blessed retreat each night since then: a warm, reassuring space to relax, gather one’s thoughts, and plan ahead.

The route so far. The blue line indicates the paddling route, the red line shows the route taken by the support vehicle. Image: Dominic Gribbin

What kayak are you paddling, and how much equipment do you carry?

I am paddling around Britain in a Rockpool Taran 16 sea kayak. It is a fast, beautifully handmade sea kayak, perfect for putting down the miles and handling heavy seas. The trade-off is stability, but it has a prodigious load capacity in its various watertight bulkheads.

I carry a kayak trolley permanently on the back deck. I have already worn out two and am constantly experimenting with new designs to better negotiate the challenges of gravel and sand beaches. As a minimum, I carry basic wild-camping equipment in case I need to spend an unexpected night ashore.

Food consists of pre-cooked rice bags, canned fish and vegetables, alongside plenty of snacks. I favor savory rather than sweet food. Coffee is my essential luxury, and I normally carry a can or two of beer!

Safety equipment is extensive. I carry a Garmin 86i Marine GPS with InReach satellite tracking, an ICOM marine handheld VHF radio with AIS and GPS, a spare VHF radio, flares and smoke signals, and a McMurdo personal locator beacon. I also carry a fully integrated Garmin Fenix 7 Pro watch, first-aid kit, spare paddles, compass, mobile phone, battery packs, head lamp, repair tape, and a Swiss Army penknife.

The kayak itself weighs 24.9kg, but the overall weight, including my dry suit, buoyancy aid, clothing, and equipment, easily reaches 35kg or more. It is a significant challenge to negotiate all this weight over an often-unfriendly shoreline. However, the kayak benefits from the additional weight when afloat.

What have been the most memorable moments along the way?

We have had numerous encounters with sea otters, hunting pods of bottlenose dolphins, and close-up encounters with bottlenose mothers and calves. There have also been golden eagles and white-tailed sea eagles, the largest raptor in the UK. Some of the most sublime moments have been the inshore sea passages through the sheltered waters of the Inner Hebrides.

Successfully rounding Cape Wrath was a truly intimidating but awe-inspiring milestone. Then there was rounding the infamous Duncansby Head and crossing the Pentland Firth near John O’Groats, finally seeing the compass turn south. The huge breeding seabird colonies off Caithness and much of Scotland’s northeast coast have been incredible. Literally tens of thousands of birds, a deafening cacophony of noise!

Right along the GB coastline, we have also met some of the warmest and most generous people.

Have there been any particularly frightening moments?

The huge seas off Strathy Point, Caithness, are probably the closest call yet. If something had gone wrong there while two kilometers offshore in those seas, I wouldn’t be writing this.

I have experienced plenty of rough and scary seas so far, but that occasion was another order of magnitude. They were enormous seas driven by Arctic swell and spring tides. They were the biggest seas I have ever paddled in. I am not in a rush to return there, despite its beauty.

You have mentioned that you are now combining freelance work with the expedition. How are you managing the financial and logistical side?

We were able to make this happen because I am self-employed. We bankrolled the expedition using our savings. The motorhome for shore support was the biggest investment. We initially calculated finances based on finishing by mid-autumn, but those weather delays cost us dearly. We ran out of money by mid-September, so I have had to return to my freelance work as a TV cameraman and juggle that with keeping this Edge of Britain expedition going until we are finished.

There is no stopping this winter. Instead, we will take advantage of every weather window.

I began paddling at age 11 when I permanently borrowed a friend’s old kayak and started exploring the ankle-deep waters of the River Ver and River Colne around St. Albans and Park Street, Hertfordshire. At 13, I started British Canoe Union training. This began my lifelong involvement with whitewater paddling on rivers around the world.

Back in the 1970s and 1980s, when I began, skills progression was funneled entirely through very actively encouraged participation in canoe slalom. Everybody who learned to paddle at club level was involved in slalom to some degree. I chose men’s C1 (Canadian singles) and competed at a national level, ranking 19th in Great Britain by the age of 18.

University changed my orientation somewhat, and the allure of traveling to exotic whitewater rivers around the world took over. Expedition whitewater paddling then became my life, and still is, alongside expedition sea kayaking. Combining this with filmmaking ultimately led directly to my career as a television cameraman.

Why did you decide to take on a circumnavigation of Britain?

The decision to attempt to paddle around the GB mainland is the culmination of a life spent kayaking. It is hard not to fall in love with the sheer beauty and allure of the world of the river and coastline, particularly here at home in the UK. This country has what is widely celebrated as some of the best sea kayaking in the world. To dream of exploring the whole GB coastline in as much detail as time and weather allow is, to me, a logical conclusion.

The actual decision came extremely late in the day, namely January 2026. This began a frantic period of organization ahead of our June 2 launch. Admittedly, April would have been better, but prior commitments meant we had to begin in June.

I chose a clockwise route around Britain, thinking (naively) that the prevailing winds would vaguely be behind us for at least half the journey. I also wanted to tackle the potentially most technically demanding section of the northwest and north coast of Scotland early, in the height of what I envisaged as long summer days. How wrong I was!

Rebecca McPhee is a freelance writer for ExplorersWeb.

Based in the UK Rebecca is a science teacher and volunteers for a number of marine charities. She enjoys open water swimming, hiking, diving, and traveling.

#8310. No-Oxygen Team Will Try Again on Everest

Last week, high winds forced the Russian team to retreat from their third trip up the West Ridge of Everest. Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and leader Andrei Vasiliev were climbing without oxygen, with no one else on the mountain. Winter is quickly approaching, but they have no intention of going home yet.

“We are at Lobuche…resting, analyzing the weather forecast. Still want to try again,” Vasiliev texted to ExplorersWeb over the weekend. The climbers had not intended to reach the summit on that latest attempt up the West Shoulder of Everest via the Lho La Pass. Vasiliev explained that they were not yet acclimatized enough to reach the top without bottled oxygen. They did expect to reach higher than before, but high winds made that impossible.

In a post on social media, member Sergey Kondrashkin recalls the latest trip up. On November 11, the team set off from their tent at the base of the West Ridge, fixing ropes in bitterly cold temperature. Contrary to forecasts, winds were light. The climbers pitched their tent at 6,500m and still had time to fix some ropes above them.

On the following morning, however, the gusts were too strong. After waiting in vain for the gale to abate, and with a forecast of even stronger winds the following day, Kondrashkin returned to the ridge, trying not to be blown away. He advanced between gusts and retrieved his two ice axes and the rope he had left behind the day before. They would need that gear for the descent.

Once at the bivouac, the climbers retrieved their tent, cached some food and fuel, and downclimbed to their Camp 1 at some 5,600m. It lies on the steep section between the Khumbu Glacier and the Lho La. Here, they pitched their tent again.

On Friday, the Russian team rappelled down to the glacier, on a “relatively safe” line to the right, where an avalanche fell as they descended.

Today, the team sits at their lodge in Lobuche and looks intently at weather forecasts. “We have not yet decided when to return to the mountain,” Vasiliev told Explorersweb. “It’s all about the weather, and the forecasts announce high winds on November 20-21.”

#8309. ‘Full Panic Mode.’ Bowhunter Tags the 205-Inch Louisiana Buck His Family Followed for 3 Seasons

Published Nov 16, 2026 2:00 PM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

For three years brothers Zack and Daniel Halbert of Bossier Parish, Louisiana, watched a nontypical buck grow into an incredible 200-class deer. They kept tabs on the buck with trail cameras and debated when it was time to shoot the high and wide whitetail.

“We never got a chance to shoot him last year,” Zack tells Outdoor Life. “Over last summer when he was still in velvet we saw on cameras that his rack had completely blown up and got huge, with lots of palmation.”

It was clear this was the season to try to kill him. The brothers hunted hard during a 23-day stint in October, with one of them in a stand every day.

“I was just the lucky one sitting that day when the buck slipped up,” says Zack, a business-studies student at Louisiana Tech University. “My brother, dad, and I put in a lot of work hunting that buck. I would not have taken this deer without their help.”

The Halberts had multiple setups around their 80-acre hunting property. Zack took the buck from a ground blind on a 48-degree morning in late October.

“The blind faced the woods, and I’m looking one way out a window, then leaned the other way, and there he was at 21 yards,” Zack says. “It’s crazy how you can go from calm and in two seconds go into full panic mode.”

Zack watched the buck for three long minutes as he waited for a broadside shot. When the buck finally turned, he drew and held at full draw for about 15 seconds. Then he let fly.

The buck took off, and Zack watched where it disappeared into the woods. Then he called his brother, dad, and girlfriend with the news.

“When I shot I was so pumped I almost shook the ground blind over. Before I got out of the blind I was trying to stop shaking enough to finish my prayer for what a blessing it was.”

Zack began trailing the deer into timber, but the blood became faint and he decided it would be best to call in a tracking dog.

“I didn’t want to mess up on this deer,” he says.

Tracker Eric Perry and his dog, Blue, arrived that evening.

“It was getting toward dusk when the dog got there and was put on the buck’s trail,” Zack says. “Blue found it in just 15 minutes. The arrow was a good hit, but there was no exit hole and so not a good blood trail.”

The deer had died in a creek, and Zack had to wade into the cold water to get his buck out. The crew dragged the deer out of the timber and loaded it into a truck and headed home. Zack estimates it was 5½ years old, and Buckmasters scorer Chris Bates measured Zack’s buck at 205 3/8 inches.

Although Buckmasters has a different scoring system than the one used by Boone and Crockett and Pope and Young Clubs (and therefore scores aren’t apples-to-apples), it’s worth noting that the largest nontypical killed with a bow in the state scored, according to P&Y records, 206 5/8 inches. That deer was taken in January 2012 by Alton McLead.

“I know my grandpa Dan, who isn’t with us anymore,” says Zack, “wouldn’t have believed his eyes if he got to see this deer.”

#8307. Why I’m Walking Away From Nursing

​I’m Cat. I work as a registered nurse, and starting in January, I’ll be trading in my scrubs for trail runners and a backpack. My husband and I are known to be spontaneous and challenge ourselves when life starts feeling boring. Packing a U-Haul with whatever fits and moving to a state we’ve never been to, hiking to the top of a mountain in Colorado to exchange vows, buying a house 14 hours away we’ve only seen pictures of online; you could say we live for the spontaneity of life. My motivation for hiking the trail goes far beyond last-minute decision-making; it comes from more recent experiences while working as a nurse.

Exchanging vows on the summit of Mount Bierstadt (14,065 feet)

​Nursing has this way of showing you just how fragile life really is. Having worked as a float tech in all units of the hospital and recently as a nurse in ICU step-down and rehab, I’ve cared for adults, both young and old, who lost their health and independence in an instant. I quickly realized I’ve been taking my own health for granted. I didn’t quite know I was in search of a challenge in life, but as always, my husband was at the driver’s seat of a new adventure. This time, it was all on me.

​It all started sitting by the fire in our backyard. My seasoned thru-hiker husband asked if I wanted to hike the Appalachian Trail; I shrugged and said okay. A week later, he suggested adding the Florida Trail first to get my trail legs ready; I quickly agreed to that, too. By the third week, he suggested I hike the entire ECT. Just like that, a casual backyard fire turned into a 4,500-mile hike.

​I’ll be hiking the Eastern Continental Trail (ECT), which is a connection of trails spanning from Florida to Canada. I decided to blog my adventures to have something to look back on and to share my travels with friends and family. I don’t know what lies ahead of me, but what I do know is I’m about to make so many memories, connections, and mistakes!

If you’d like to follow along with the journey, I’ll be sharing updates, photos, and stories right here while I head north.

​The very basic core of a man’s living spirit is his passion for adventure. The joy of life comes from our encounters with new experiences, and hence there is no greater joy than to have an endlessly changing horizon, for each day to have a new and different sun.

—Chris McCandless (​Alexander Supertramp)

#8305. Officials Blame Climate Change for Glacier Collapse That Killed 17

Russian authorities are now attributing the September 6 disaster on 5,047m Mount Mizhirgi in the northern Caucasus to climate-related destabilization of a hanging glacier.

A half-million cubic meter avalanche struck a military group undergoing mountain training, killing 17 and injuring 10. Another 10 were unharmed and made it down the mountain on their own.

The impact generated a powerful blast of displaced air that reportedly threw some victims 200m to 300m down the slope before burying them. As we reported at the time, helicopter pilot Alexander Davydov caught the avalanche on video.

Eldar Khashkhozhev of the Russian Ministry of Emergency Situations explained that warmer temperatures melted the protective blanket of snow, exposing parts of the glacier. This weakened the ice support that had glued enormous masses of snow and ice in place for decades.

A helicopter inspection of the region’s snow conditions the month before found no cause for concern, and some officials insist the catastrophe was unpredictable. However, climber Dmitry Polyakov, who was in the region at the time, disputed the idea that the glacier posed no danger. He said climbers had long recognized its instability and generally avoided approaching it in large groups.

The Mizhirgi Glacier against Mizhirgi East and West peaks, site of September’s catastrophic glacial collapse. Photo: Shutterstock

The key points of Khashkhozhev’s explanation were:

Rising temperatures have raised the altitude of permanent snow cover.

Previously protected sections of the glacier became exposed, weakening the supporting ice beneath the hanging masses.

Eventually, gravity overcame that support and triggered a collapse that struck the training group.

This was the largest climbing disaster in the country since 2002, when another glacier collapse in North Ossetia, located between the Black and Caspian Seas, killed 125 people, including local residents.

With major landslides in summer and the possibility of glacial collapse at other times of the year throughout the world, mountaineers will have to adjust their behavior, as previously safe areas become potentially deadly.

#8303. Alaska Considers ‘Unprecedented’ Closure of Public Land to Hunting, Trapping Along Controversial Ambler Road

Published Nov 16, 2026 4:38 PM EST

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

The state of Alaska may soon decide to close more than 400 square miles to hunting and trapping in anticipation of a controversial mining road. The decision would be part of a push by the Alaska Industrial Development and Export Authority to build a road creating private access to a future mining district focused on copper and zinc deposits.

While the Ambler Road itself has faced continuous opposition from hunting and conservation groups for its potential to fragment one of the largest remaining caribou herds, among other fish and habitat issues, the recent development is creating even more consternation.

“It’s unprecedented,” says Mary Glaves, Alaska program manager for Backcountry Hunters and Anglers. “We’re supposed to allow for balanced use of all of our resources. This would show preference to one resource over another.”

The proposal, which the Alaska Board of Game will consider during an online meeting Friday, would close 1 mile on either side of the 211-mile proposed road in northern Alaska to all hunting and trapping. It first became public in February and is part of a memorandum of understanding between several Alaskan native corporations and the state. The proposed closure is part of a “subsistence safeguard,” according to a story in the Alaska Beacon. Subsistence hunters could still cross through the road corridor to access other legal hunting grounds.

The hunting and trapping ban would begin July 1, 2029, and remain in place through at least Jan. 1, 2036, regardless of when or even if the road is built, Glaves says.

The Board of Game considered formalizing the MOU in a July meeting, and opposition was fierce, says Glaves. Still, many Alaskan organizations could not prepare comment because the meeting was in the middle of fishing season. As a result, the board tabled the discussion until its formal meeting in January.

A few months later, the Alaska Fish and Game commissioner announced another special meeting Nov. 20 to discuss the project, allowing only written public comment and no oral testimony.

“That isn’t illegal,” Glaves says, “but it’s not in the best interest of engaging the public.”

Even more importantly, if the closure passes, it tells Alaskans that state public land can be shut down to access at the request of an anticipated industry and with no stated biological need.

The road has not been built, and there’s some question about whether or not Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, the Democratic governor-elect, will support the project. He has not stated a position publicly but has said he will carefully evaluate money spent by the state. The Industrial Development and Export Authority, an economic development arm of the state, would be responsible for building the road. The Alaska Wilderness League, which opposes the project, estimates it could cost the state more than $2 billion including construction, maintenance, and financing.

The preemptive nature of the closure is particularly troubling to conservation groups.

Read Next: The Ambler Road Project Would Jeopardize One of the Last Great Wilderness Hunts in America

“There is no compelling reason to establish these restrictions years before the project is constructed or in the absence of demonstrated need,” she wrote on Nov. 4. “Doing so would also set a troubling precedent of using the Board’s time and public resources to evaluate hypothetical impacts of projects that may never materialize, rather than addressing actual wildlife management and public access concerns as they arise.”

Christine Peterson is a freelance writer based in southeast Wyoming covering hunting, fishing, outdoor recreation, wildlife and the environment for Outdoor Life, High Country News, National Geographic and others.

#8302. Never-Say-Die Climbers Will Try Everest Again This Weekend

Despite a forecast of high winds on November 21 and 22, Andrei Vasiliev, Sergey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov have decided to begin a new attempt on the West Ridge of Everest on Sunday.

The three stubborn Russians will again proceed via the West Ridge without bottled oxygen, support, or any other living soul on the mountain.

The forecasts warn of very high winds all weekend. Nevertheless, they will start up on Sunday, November 22, although that is the day with the strongest winds forecast.

“That day, we will remain low on the mountain and climb to our Camp 1 at 5,600m,” Sergey Kondrashkin wrote.  “From there, we will push upward when the weather improves and the winds die down, aiming to descend around November 28.”

This means the team does not intend to summit quite yet. The goal is to acclimatize by reaching 7,500m and then return to their headquarters in Lobuche.

“The question is, will we manage to complete the summit push within the time frame of our permit, which expires on December 15, and will the weather cooperate?” said Kondrashkin.

The fall season on Everest usually lasts until the end of November, since December 1 marks the start of Nepal’s winter climbing season. However, the permit dates may have been extended for this team, which is climbing off the normal route.

Once winter settles in, it will be the turn of Jost Kobusch of Germany, who will attempt to solo Everest in winter along the same route the Russians are now attempting.

On their third and latest trip up the mountain so far, the team only reached 6,700m before hurricane-force winds up to 130kph forced them down, according to former team member Natalyia Belyankina. Belyankina had to leave the expedition for health reasons but has stayed in touch with the others.

#8298. Te Araroa day 20: Catching up with friendly faces

26km, Ruakākā Motor Camp to Waorahi Campsite

After my day off the previous day, I was keen to get walking. The weather was thankfully looking better – the threat of a few showers, perhaps, but nowhere near as bad as the day before. Feeling energetic, I thought I might end up doing a bigger day and pushing all the way through to Mangawhai Heads, 39km away. Alternatively, I could stay at a free campsite in 26 kilometres. I set out at my usual not-especially-early time, and headed to the beach. The day would start with 5km of beach walking before heading inland.

The tide was pretty much all the way in, so I had to walk on soft sand which was pretty annoying. As I walked, I kept getting whiffs of pee. I couldn’t work out where it was coming from, but eventually realised that my right hand smelled of pee and traced the smell back to the strap of my hiking pole. And then I realised what must have happened. You see, one of the great but not often discussed advantages of the Durston X-Mid tent is that the vestibule is large enough to squat and pee in. On a rainy night when you just don’t want to leave your tent, that can be a great advantage. And so it had gone the previous night. I had spent the day drinking fruit juice, eating grapes, and chugging water. I’m sure this was great for my hydration, but it meant that I needed to pee in the night, and it was raining. Presumably, the strap of my hiking pole got caught in the cross-fire and ended up with pee on it. And now it was on my hand. Excellent.

Somewhat perturbed but with not much I could do about it, I continued along the beach. Far in the distance, I could see some little figures that looked like hikers. I couldn’t figure out who they could be though, as there were only two and the hiker trio I had been with the day before would have been unlikely to split up so soon. I continued along my way, and gradually got closer – I’m a pretty speedy walker, and my curiosity motivated me to walk quickly. As I neared them, I started to recognise one of the figures. It looked like they were wearing Annabel’s distinctive flowy shorts, and once I figured that out I was almost certain that one of them was Annabel. And the other person looked like Lindsay to me. Now it made sense – I had kind of forgotten that these two, and a number of others who I had previously been hiking with, had got an AirBnB in Ruakākā for a day off. I would have joined them had I known that I would also be taking a zero the previous day, but since that wasn’t my plan, I had stayed at the campground.

Annabel and Lindsay in the distance – this was when I recognised them, although they were more distinct in real life

Beach walking with Lindsay and Annabel – photo by Sinéad

Happy to see some friends, I put the boosters on and caught up to them fairly quickly. We soon also caught Sinéad, who had been taking a dip in the sea. I explained my ‘pee stick’ problem and we had a good laugh about it. The others threatened to make Pee Sticks my trail name, but I vetoed that pretty quickly! As we were standing around, a man came jogging barefoot down the beach towards us. He stopped by us, asked the now-familiar question (‘are you doing that big walk?’) and asked why we didn’t go barefoot on the beach. We told him that our feet needed more support for long kilometres of beach walking, especially with weight on our backs. He looked unconvinced, but wished us luck and jogged away. To be fair, he could probably walk the length of 90 Mile beach without shoes. But I certainly couldn’t!

It was good to catch up with the others about their day off, and I was having a great time walking with friends again. I realised that I was not going to go all the way to Mangawhai Heads that day – I would much rather hang out with this lot and have a fun time. We had all heard through the grapevine that there was a cafe in Waipu that gave hikers free coffee, so that was our destination for the morning. After the beach, there was a bit of gravel road and then a kilometre or two of main road to walk down to reach Waipu. I was walking with Sinéad and we were chatting away. At one point I looked behind and the others weren’t there. Had we really walked that fast? ‘They probably hitched,’ said Sinéad. Aha. I had forgotten that hitching was a thing – it would never have occurred to me on this short of a road section! But fair enough, there’s no need to walk on busy main roads if you don’t want to.

We got into Waipu, which was surprisingly popping for a small place on a random Wednesday. I made a beeline for the public toilets to wash the pee smell off my hand and gear, then headed to Logan McClean cafe where legend has it, hikers get a free hot drink. The others were already there, along with the hiker trio from my day off. The lady at the counter at the cafe asked if I was walking too, which saved me from the awkwardness of having to say ‘Sooo, I heard you do free drinks for hikers?’ In addition to my coffee, I got a couple of slices. I couldn’t choose and figured I would take one away with me. We sat outside the cafe for a bit, and Sven turned up too. He hadn’t heard that there was free coffee here, so had bought one at another cafe. But then of course he had to make use of the freebie so got another! A few people came up to talk to us, including an older guy who had done the TA a few years ago. The others had various things to buy at the Four Square and the pharmacy, and then we were back on our way.

Apricot crumble and ginger macadamia slices – I thought I would take one of them away. That didn’t happen, shocker

The next section looked to be mostly road walking. Sven (ever the hitching fan) and Lindsay hopped in a car, but me, Annabel and Sinéad decided to give the road a go. I wasn’t keen to hitch at all, as this would already be a shorter day for me and I was full of energy from my day off. Things started out promisingly, with a pavement to walk on through the rest of the town. But soon, the pavement stopped and it looked as though we would be on tarmac. Then I happened to glance across the road and saw a TA sign leading to a bike path. Great! The bike path turned out to be reasonably scenic, and we were happy we chose to walk.

At one point, I had to stop to change my sock. I had washed the sand out of my shoes and socks from the end of the last day, but with the rain they hadn’t had a chance to dry. This morning, I had wanted a dry pair of socks, but after the recent death of a sock I only had 1.5 pairs to work with and decided to use my bed socks. They’re hiking socks anyway, but on TA so far I had been using toe socks. But I figured it was worth a go. Unfortunately, it was becoming apparent that I needed toe socks – the toes on my left foot were rubbing and I could tell I would get blisters. Happily, the remaining sock from the half pair was a left one, so I was able to change that out and keep my right sock as it was. I didn’t think there was anything particularly odd about this, but when the others saw my odd socks at camp later they seemed to think it was an abomination.

My odd socks at camp later – is this really so strange? It was working for me!

After a bit of effort, I caught Annabel and Sinead again after my sock stop. The bike path went on a bit longer before the trail turned up a side road. We had to walk on the road this time, but it was a quiet road, and quite scenic as it wound its way up the hill. At one point it became a gravel road, and we stopped for a lunch break. After a while on the gravel road, which became progressively narrower and more overgrown, we reached the final 2km to the campsite and the first real track of the day! We knew there was some weather due to be coming in later, and as I walked up (and down) the track, I could hear thunder rumbling in the distance. I was keen to get to camp sooner rather than later, but after the day of gentle climbing on the road, the track felt exceedingly steep and hilly, and my calves were definitely not prepared for such a workout.

Eventually, I popped out of the trees and reached the campsite. Having been here before, I remembered the site as nice but not overly flat and a bit exposed. I was happy to see that there was more flat area than I remembered, although the majority of the site was on quite a hill. The views out across the sea were great. Lindsay was pitching her tent as I arrived, and I pitched mine pretty close, concious of the sloping ground and the other two behind me.

It was funny how the surfaced road stopped so abruptly

Sven had decided to continue on to Waipu after his short, hitching-heavy day. It was only 3.30pm at this point and if it hadn’t been for the approaching weather and the good company at this campsite, I might have done the same. As I expressed to the others, I’ve been feeling a bit of tension between wanting the physical challenge of pushing for some bigger days, and wanting the trip to last as long as possible so I can enjoy it as much as possible. I think as I move southwards I’ll naturally end up with some bigger days, especially where there are more camping options. Right now, most places are spaced 20-25km apart, and I don’t feel ready for 40-50km days yet! But at the same time, 25km days on easier terrain, like this day, are feeling easy and I get to camp feeling like I haven’t done enough.

As well as the people I had been walking with that day, Bart and Anica were at the campsite. I hadn’t met Anica before, as apparently she has been skipping around a bit. But she seemed cool and we all sat around the table in the shelter, chatting and cooking dinner as we watched the storm roll in. It was a fun place to sit, as we could see bands of rain moving across the ocean towards us. It seemed like the worst of it missed us, but we did get a few heavy showers over the course of the evening. There was a logbook at that campsite, and it provided some good entertainment over the course of the evening. We made plans to hike out at 7 the next morning, for some reason, and found a trail host in Mangawhai that offered camping for significantly cheaper than the holiday park.

This entry made me laugh so much, I had to do a dramatic reading for the others

#8296. Jost Kobusch to Train For Everest on Difficult, Dangerous Lhotse Shar

Jost Kobusch of Germany has moved to the Khumbu Valley to finish his acclimatization before attempting to solo winter Everest, beginning on December 22. His preparations include reaching 8,000m on a different peak.

Kobusch is now in Chukhung village, from which he climbed 6,165m Island Peak (Imja Tse) yesterday. He spent the night at 6,000m, topped out again today, and went back down, as shown in his live tracker. He told ExplorersWeb that he will now rest for a few days in Lukla and then hike up the valley again to inspect conditions on his next acclimatization goal: the difficult Lhotse Shar (8,383m).

Kobusch’s climb on Island Peak as shown in his tracker today.

“My plan is not to summit but to tag 8,000m up its flank, before heading for Everest,” he said.

Lhotse Shar is one of the main points of the Lhotse ridge, and it is climbed from south side of the mountain, with Chukhung as the starting point. The main options are to climb the southeastern flank of the Shar itself or try a direct line up the formidable south face of Lhotse.

Neither of them is easy, and the upper sections are statistically dangerous. According to Wikipedia, Lhotse Shar has the highest fatality rate of all principal or secondary 8,000m peaks. For every two climbers who summit, one person dies attempting to.

Lhotse and its various points, as seen from the south. Graphic by Gorskie Mapy

The Austrian expedition that first reached the summit of Lhotse Shar (from the Southeast Ridge) in 1970 set four altitude camps, the uppermost at 7,600m. They used supplemental oxygen on their summit push. “Almost the whole of the route from below Camp 1 to Camp 3 was fixed with rope, as climbing was very difficult,” they reported in the AAJ.

Kobusch will not have to deal with the nearly vertical terrain and cornices near the summit, but will have to face difficult mixed terrain and uncertain conditions if he wants to venture up to 8,000m. He will not use bottled oxygen, and as far as we know, he will climb on his own.

Kobusch plans to reach the base of Everest on December 22 and solo the mountain in winter without oxygen, via the West Ridge — the same line currently being attempted by a Russian team.

This is Kobusch’s fourth attempt, and he is willing to try to reach the summit this time. However, when asked about it, he admits he does not know if such a feat is actually possible. “Every expedition, every training session, every difficult decision has been part of preparing myself for what I know will be the biggest challenge of my life,” he admits.

Kobusch’s is not the only confirmed climb this winter. Denis Urubko of Russia is reportedly preparing to climb Broad Peak in winter, possibly starting at the end of this year and continuing through January and February. On social media, Urubko mentioned he will be climbing with Vitaliy Skel. However, details of his route have not been confirmed.

Simone Moro of Italy has not decided whether to try Manaslu again this winter. He told ExplorersWeb he is still considering his plans while observing the “crazy weather this season.” Moro attempted Manaslu in fall to acclimatize and become familiar with the terrain. However, like every other team, he had to call off the attempt due to dangerous conditions following extremely heavy snowfall. Moro wants to climb the peak in alpine style.

#8291. The Paradox of Seeking First Ascents in Western Nepal

Western Nepal has plenty of unclimbed 6,000m peaks, and Fredrik Strang of Sweden and Sindre Kolbjornsgard of Norway went there planning to climb one. In the end, they settled for a slightly lower but equally memorable experience. It showed again that adventure goes beyond first ascents.

What I remember most clearly about that narrow summit is not the grade, the exposure, or the possibility of being first. It is the silence. No helicopters. No voices from a fixed-rope queue. No machinery, no aircraft, no distant sound of a settlement. Only the two of us, a serrated horizon, and an unfamiliar feeling that the mountain had asked a question rather than supplied an answer.

Sindre Kolbjornsgard, left, and Fredrik Strang. Photo: Fredrik Strang

After 18 expeditions to 8,000’ers and witnessing the evolution (or devolution) of climbing on these peaks’ normal routes, Strang and his partner knew they wanted something different. Quoting Ed Viesturs, Strang said: “The point is to climb, not just to summit.” With that in mind, the climbers set four criteria for their objectives:

Several route options face the climbers’ base camp tent. Photo: Fredrik Strang

Strang noted that there are many unclimbed peaks left in Nepal, but they were looking for a compelling climb, not just a dull summit for the record. They finally found one that satisfied their criteria, but then, as with so many other teams in Nepal this fall, harsh weather put their original objective out of reach. Not to mention that traveling Western Nepal is anything but simple.

“Our intended destination was in the Nyalu Lek area north of Simikot,” Strang revealed. “We planned to cross Nyalu La, a pass around 5,000m, with a support party that included porters and pack animals.

“Getting from Surkhet to Simikot took two rough days by road, with landslides having damaged or obliterated sections of the route. At Simikot, we learned that Nyalu La was probably impassable. Even reaching the place where we planned to start trekking had been uncertain.”

When they did reach the area, they confirmed that their planned peak was not an option. Hiking further down the valley, they pitched their tent at Phendol Kermi Camp. Snow had covered the trails beyond, but they simply had no time or money to move to some other region in Nepal. Instead, they decided to explore whatever was close to their camp.

During their stay, they encountered Mick Fowler and Victor Saunders of the UK. Bad weather had likewise spoiled the British pair’s plan to attempt an unclimbed 6,000m peak farther east, known only as Peak 6010, according to Mount Everest Foundation.. This would have been their second attempt on that peak. Ironically, dry conditions spoiled their 2025 attempt. This time, too much snow forced them back. Read more on the British climbers’ adventure here:

On October 6, Strang and Kolbjornsgard made their first acclimatization climb on a 5,177m peak at 30°20′49.82″N, 82°03′54.82″E. They found no records of any previous ascent.

“From base camp, the mountain looked straightforward, and lower down, it largely was,” Strang recalls. “Steep grass, mud, and broken rock led toward the upper slopes. But at about 4,500m, the route disappeared beneath knee-deep snow, then waist-deep snow, and every step became a small excavation.”

In the following days, they scouted and flew their drone down side valleys, looking for possibilities. Their second peak was 5,227m in altitude, located at 30°07′50.86″N, 81°41′56.58″E. Again, there were no records of previous ascents. Parts of it were far from fun.

“Below 4,500m, progress was tolerable, but above that, we were back to forcing our way through knee-deep, sometimes chest-deep snow,” Strang wrote. “A tremendous amount of work for very little enjoyment.”

Luckily, the climb improved once they reached the summit ridge, on relatively easy mixed rock and ice, which they assessed at PD+.

“Fowler and Saunders climbed the mountain several days later and found an easier way to descend and reascend the step on its western side,” Strang noted. “Their solution was a reminder that the first line a team takes is not necessarily the best one.”

Still, the peak that most drew the climbers’ attention was a remarkable 5,337m tooth of rock above Yangchya Lake at approximately 30°07′09.36″N, 81°41′21.15″E.

“We began calling it Daara Peak — a name inspired by the Nepali word for a projecting tooth or fang and by the mountain’s striking shape,” Strang said. He notes that the name is provisional while they await a response from the authorities about their suggestion.

Strang describes the peak as “a saber-toothed tiger’s canine protruding from a mass of rock. The terminal pinnacle was about eight meters high, overhanging and sharply defined against the sky.”

The climbers about to reach what they called Daara Peak. Drone photo: Brizendra Bhattarai

The problem was approaching the peak in deep, heavy snow from Yangchya Lake. They failed on their first attempt to tackle its northeast headwall. After waiting out another snowy spell, the climbers returned for a second attempt on October 17-18.

The climbers dealt with 250m of rather poor rock, a complex approach to the headwall across a bergschrund with soft snow, and the uncertainty of moving on unfamiliar terrain. They had no idea of the difficulties ahead or whether they could protect the passages ahead on their way to the summit. The route included vertical granite walls, with cracks adequate for cams, some mixed terrain with the crux at M6, a steep couloir, and then the summit ridge: a granite edge with some 30cm of snow on top.

Climbing terrain on Daara Peak. Photo: Fredrik Strang

Rather than technical difficulty, the section was delicate due to exposure and a lack of comfortable belay stations. Yet, the climbers reached the summit on October 18, including the top of the final pinnacle, thanks to a crack in the rock.

Strang admits that the climbing details suggest a rather straightforward ascent: a 5,337m summit via its northeast side in five pitches with difficulties up to M6. However, Strang judges the climb on a different scale. “The technical crux was behind us, but it was the part I remember most vividly,” he explained. “It was the silence.”

Strang and Kolbjornsgard’s route up Daara Peak. Photo: Fredrik Strang

On many of the 8,000m peaks I have climbed, the human presence has become part of the landscape: camps, radio calls, fixed ropes, queues, and the distant sound of aircraft. Up here, none of that reached us. Mountains extended in every direction. There was no audience, no ceremony, no one to confirm that we had accomplished anything at all.

Strang also reflects on the paradox: They enjoyed the wild terrain but, if every climber chases solitude by visiting these last remote valleys, the character of these places will inevitably change. For Strang, the question is not to ban access. However, he says:

Perhaps some summits should remain untouched — not because we lack the skill or courage to reach them, but because future generations deserve to inherit mountains that have not all been reduced to objectives.

The climb from the ridge. Photo: Fredrik Strang

Angela Benavides graduated university in journalism and specializes in high-altitude mountaineering and expedition news. She has been writing about climbing and mountaineering, adventure and outdoor sports for 20+ years.

Prior to that, Angela Benavides spent time at/worked at a number of local and international media. She is also experienced in outdoor-sport consultancy for sponsoring corporations, press manager and communication executive, and a published author.

ExplorersWeb is part of AllGear Digital's portfolio of media brands.

#8289. The Incredible Hunt for the C.W. Shelton Buck, One of the Widest Bucks in the World

Published Nov 16, 2026 6:13 PM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

This story, “I Shot Big Red,” appeared in the January 1967 issue of Outdoor Life. Shelton’s buck is now the 20th biggest typical whitetail ever taken in Kentucky, according to the Boone and Crockett Club. At the time, however, it was the biggest ever taken in Kentucky. It also had a wider inside and outside spread than any deer on the books, including the then-world-record deer.

At 2 o’clock in the afternoon on November 28, 1964, I was ready to give up the dream of a lifetime. The rain, which had been steady since before dawn, suddenly stopped, and the woods of northern Todd County, Kentucky, were still. I was 20 feet up in a huge sycamore, watching a deer runway that meandered through thick brush. I’d been half-wet most of the day, and I felt another case of chills coming on.

I might as well quit, I thought. I’m not going to see Big Red, and I probably won’t see any other deer.

My thoughts seemed logical, but another line of reasoning wouldn’t be denied. This was Todd County’s first deer season in modern times, and the season was for this day only. So far as Big Red was concerned, I had good reason to believe he was the best trophy whitetail buck in North America. Besides, I’m mighty stubborn when it comes to deer hunting. I decided to stay in that tree till dark.

In front of me, to the north and 30 yards away, a tiny creek flowed through a heavily wooded east-west valley. The runway crossed the creek and continued into dense thickets. I couldn’t see the thickets’ far edge, but I knew the growth thinned against a hillside that topped out alongside a stubble cornfield 200 yards away. The cornfield was 40 yards wide and bordered a little-used gravel road. Across the road was 40 acres of tangled cedars, the thickest cover in the area. I figured any deer leaving those cedars would use the runway I was watching.

Around 2:30 a twig snapped behind me, to the south. Then I heard branches rubbing together and sounds resembling a squirrel digging in the ground. I knew I was listening to a deer.

The sounds were a few yards off the runway. In another minute they became more distinguishable, and I knew the animal was working toward me. I had two choices: remain motionless in hopes the deer would move past me, or try to inch my way around so I’d face south.

Though the leaves were off the trees, I figured I had an excellent chance of moving without being seen. I was standing on a huge branch, but I was tight against the trunk. Deer don’t normally look up, so I also had that advantage. In addition, I figured the deer was feeding and not alerted to immediate danger. I moved as cautiously as possible.

It took a few minutes to make my move. Now I was facing south. Surprisingly, I could still hear the same sounds, but I couldn’t see any movement.

The sounds kept coming closer. Then, as if by magic, there he was. I saw antlers and legs at the same instant, about 30 yards away. The buck was pawing at acorns. I couldn’t get a clear view of his antlers, and I didn’t dare risk a shot through that thick brush. There wasn’t much I could do except wait.

After what seemed like hours, he suddenly tossed his head up. He seemed to be looking straight at me. His rack was massive, but I knew instantly it didn’t belong to Big Red. I was sure the buck had caught a glimpse of me or winded me.

I better take him, I thought. Time is running out.

My .44 Magnum Ruger carbine was braced against the trunk. I started lining the crosswires of my Weaver scope on his chest. Then, through my variable-power scope, I made an amazing discovery. That buck wasn’t looking up at me at all; he was staring on the level along the runway toward the north.

Now the eight-pointer relaxed and dropped his head to feed again. I heard the same sounds that had startled him. To the north, behind me now, I heard another deer. I glanced over my shoulder and got the second biggest shock of my life. Big Red, in all his glory, was walking toward my tree stand. The monstrous buck was in clear view, 50 yards away and moving down the runway. There was no question about his identity.

I had seen him two years ago when we had come face to face under the most dramatic conditions. We had startled each other that time. Now I had all the cards. Or did I? I was in no position to shoot. If that buck was alerted to the slightest suspicion, he’d bound into the thickets and disappear.

This dream situation had been in the making for a long time. I guess it really started when I was nine years old, the day I shot my first squirrel. After stalking the gray for hours, I knocked it off a stump with my brother Rudy’s .22. I decided then and there I wanted to become the world’s best hunter. That boyhood ambition has never dimmed, though it’s been realistically tempered by maturity. At that time my family lived in the town of Mayfield, in southwestern Kentucky. There was plenty of small game and birds, but no deer.

By the time I got a chance to go deer hunting, I discovered I wasn’t much of a hunter after all.

By the time I was in high school, I was addicted to duck hunting. The area around Mayfield is laced with creeks, rivers, and potholes. It was a duck paradise. I taught myself how to call by sneaking up on flocks of waterfowl and listening to their various calls. I’d go hunting before and after school every day during the season. I practically lived outdoors. But by the time I got a chance to go deer hunting, I discovered I wasn’t much of a hunter after all.

I’m 26 now and live in Bowling Green, where I work as a real estate salesman and auctioneer. My wife and I have a daughter, four, and a son, two.

Kentucky’s first modern deer season opened in 1956, when I was still a teenager. I didn’t get a chance to hunt deer until 1959, but nobody ever dreamed about deer hunting more than I did.

Looking back, I realize I started my first season as quite a stupid deer hunter. I had no experience, and I’d never seen a deer in my life. The 1959 season lasted three days, and I hunted every one of them from dawn to dark. After it was all over, my record was unblemished: I still hadn’t seen a deer. I’m not sure I even saw a fresh track.

Three months before the 1960 season opened, I started scouting my hunting territory on weekends. With six weeks to go, I stepped up my scouting trips to every couple of days. I found runways and beds, examined browse conditions, and located the “use” areas of three herds of whitetails. It all paid off. I killed a fat doe from a tree stand just after dawn on the opening day of the season.

I missed the 1961 season because of a session with Uncle Sam, but I didn’t lose contact with shooting. My ability with a rifle was good enough to win me an instructor’s rating, and I had charge of an army rifle range for 10 months.

In 1962 and 1963, I collected my second and third whitetails. I shot both of them while sneaking silently into bedding areas I’d discovered on scouting trips. My 1962 deer bolted from thick brush 80 yards away, and I dropped him with a single bullet. My third deer, a six-pointer, heard me pussyfooting along, but I saw him before he spotted me. He went down in his tracks.

After I killed my first deer, I studied taxidermy and began mounting deer heads for my friends. I mounted the head of my big six-pointer, but every time I looked at it I dreamed of the day when those six points would be dwarfed by a much larger rack. My dream had plenty of substance because by this time I’d seen Big Red.

We met in October, 1962, while I was living in the town of Elkton, Todd County. I’d heard that the county might be opened to deer hunting, so I started scouting likely areas. I’d done some business with H. Sweeney, a local farmer, and he’d told me he frequently saw deer crossing his fields.

On one of my scouting trips, I found a heavily traveled runway through a hilly area of oak, poplar, hickory, and cedar. The runway was pocked with fresh tracks, and I followed it down through the hills and across a valley to where it led into a rye field. Where the field met the woods, a huge oak tree offered a perfect stand. I decided to climb the tree and see what moved along the runway toward evening.

About 5 p.m. I heard some deer coming through the woods. It was a warm, quiet day, and the trees were still in full foliage, so I heard them for a long time before I saw them. Shortly, three deer walked below me and went out into the rye field to feed. I watched them for half an hour. Then I heard another deer. He moved steadily to the last bit of cover, then stopped.

I made out the partial outline of a huge deer. The whitetail stood motionless for a full five minutes; then he stepped into the field and joined the other animals. He had an eight-point rack and was the biggest deer I’d ever seen.

Across the pond, 20 yards away on top of the opposite bank, stood the most magnificent whitetail buck in all the world.

Then I heard dogs barking. They were chasing something, and the sounds kept coming closer. A six-point buck suddenly burst out of the woods, ran under my tree, and joined the other deer. As if on signal, they all bolted out of sight.

I never did see the dogs or any more deer, though I stayed in the tree till dusk. I’d traveled farther than I thought, and it was dark before I got halfway back to my car. I decided to bypass the woods and stay in the fields. It was this decision that set up the chance meeting with Big Red.

I was crossing a fescue field when I approached a man-made stock pond. Banks, about 10 feet high, had been bulldozed around the pond to collect and hold water. I could have walked around the embankment, but I decided to walk along the top of it. A full moon had just cleared the horizon, and the landscape was bathed with an eerie beauty. I went up to the top of the bank and got the shock of my life. Across the pond, 20 yards away on top of the opposite bank, stood the most magnificent whitetail buck in all the world.

The huge animal was silhouetted against the moon in fantastic beauty. I guess we saw each other in the same instant, and we both froze, each sizing up the other.

I remember my breath going out in a gasp. My first thought was that I was looking at somebody’s tame elk. Then I knew the animal had to be a deer. His size didn’t awe me so much as did the tremendous spread of his antlers.

We must have stared at each other for seconds. Then the monster buck snorted, whirled, and bolted down the bank and across the field. About 75 yards away, he leaped a five-foot fence. Then he stopped and looked back. I took a few steps toward him, and he trotted into some woods.

I was talking to myself when I got back to the farmer’s yard where I’d parked my car. I went up to the house and knocked on the door. He didn’t seem very impressed when I exclaimed, “I’ve just seen the biggest buck in Kentucky!”

“That’s Big Red,” he said. “I’ve seen him a few times. You can’t mistake him. He’s a lot bigger than an ordinary deer. His face is sort of reddish. That’s why we call him Big Red. The local farmers know about him, and you’re going to have plenty of company if you figure on hunting that buck.”

As it turned out, Todd County wasn’t open for deer hunting in 1962 or 1963. Kentucky controls its whitetail population by allowing hunting only in counties where the herds have built up to the carrying capacity of available deer range. In 1956 (the first year that deer hunting had been allowed since 1911) only 27 of the state’s 120 counties were open to shooting. In that season 6,000 hunters killed 1,300 whitetails. By comparison, 14,000 hunters bagged 4,100 deer in 1965. The 1966 population was estimated at well over 50,000 deer, and hunting was allowed in 74 counties.

All of this had its beginning in 1950 when the state began its stocking program with deer bought from Pennsylvania. Original stockings were made in Mammoth Cave National Park and Federal Wildlife refuges. With a ban on hunting, these herds multiplied so rapidly that certain areas became overrun with deer. Live-trapping crews thinned out the overpopulated sections and stocked the deer in other areas that had heavy browse conditions. As these herds build to huntable populations, additional counties are opened to hunting.

In the summer of 1964, the Kentucky Department of Fish and Wildlife Resources announced that Todd County would have its first deer season, a one-day hunt on November 28. I told my brother Rudy about Big Red, and we planned to hunt him together. We didn’t get much sleep the night before the season opened, and we left for our hunting area at 3 a.m.

A few changes had taken place during the two years since I’d met Big Red. The monster buck had moved from the Sweeney farm to adjoining woodlands owned by farmer Ross Laster. The deer’s travel routes had also changed, but I knew all about this because I knew Ross well and hadn’t relaxed my scouting trips. I hadn’t seen the buck a second time, but I’d found his tracks many times, and some of the local farmers had seen him just a month earlier.

Dawn was breaking when Rudy and I drove down a gravel road toward Ross’s farm. A mile from our destination, a four-point buck jumped across the road ahead of us, ran to the far edge of a small stubble cornfield and stopped.

“Get your rifle and nail him,” Rudy said as he braked the car.

“No, you take him,” I answered. Neither of us made a move, and the buck walked slowly out of sight. While we wouldn’t admit it, both Rudy and I weren’t the least bit interested in shooting that buck.

We drove to the farmhouse, and Ross had news.

“That bunch of deer are traveling new runways,” he said. “The best one is about a mile down the road by a cornfield where. . . .”

“That’s where we just saw a buck,” I interrupted. “There’s a bunch of cedars across the road.”

“That’s the place,” Ross said. “I’d forget your other plans and pick a couple of stands along that runway.”

That’s exactly what we did. Half an hour later, I found the big sycamore I mentioned in the beginning. Rudy decided to follow the runway toward some heavily wooded ridges half a mile away.

The air rasped into my throat with such suddenness that I momentarily feared he’d heard me. But he gave no sign of caution. He raised his head, walked through the shallow creek, and came directly toward my tree.

About 8 o’clock, it started raining hard. By 8:30 I was so wet I went back to the car, changed clothes, and put on a yellow rainsuit. I was almost back to the sycamore when I heard shots from Rudy’s area. I walked up on a ridge and found Rudy all excited.

“I shot at a buck with a brushpile rack,” he said. “I was curled up under a tree trying to stay dry when I heard a deer coming down the runway behind me. I turned around and we spotted each other at the same time. The buck bolted, and I cut loose with three shots. I lost his tracks right here. He sure was a big one!”

Rudy was a mighty disappointed deer hunter. He’s 35 and one of the best outdoorsmen I know. He’s been a hunting nut all his life, and he taught me how to hunt and fish when I was a boy. He lives in Mayfield where he works as a heavy-equipment operator. He’s married and has two teenage sons.

Rudy went back to his stand, and I stillhunted till noon. We met at the car for lunch, stillhunted another hour, then returned to our stands. It wasn’t long after that when I glanced over my shoulder and saw Big Red.

I don’t remember any trace of buck fever, but I do recall coldly analyzing the situation. I studied every bit of cover between myself and the deer. About 40 yards from my tree stand, a clump of cedars edged the runway. Big Red would have to pass behind that clump. When he did, I’d turn around.

My change in position came off like clockwork. When the animal appeared again he was unsuspicious, and I was in perfect shooting position with my scope lined up on his chest. I decided against squeezing the trigger. I wanted him to come as close as possible.

At the creek 30 yards away, the trophy buck stopped for a drink. The suspense was terrible. I used this moment of his relaxed alertness to suck in a deep breath. The air rasped into my throat with such suddenness that I momentarily feared he’d heard me. But he gave no sign of caution. He raised his head, walked through the shallow creek, and came directly toward my tree.

Suddenly he stopped, turned his head toward his backtrack, tilted his nose, and tested the air. Then he swung his massive antlers forward and walked behind a couple of cedars where he stopped dead still. I had a feeling he was getting nervous.

He might bolt at any second, I thought. As soon as he steps from behind those cedars, I’m going to shoot.

The range was now 25 yards, and there was no question about his increased caution. His face peeked from behind the cedars. Then that unbelievable rack. Again he stood motionless. Suddenly he broke into a fast trot.

The crosswires settled at the base of his neck, and my rifle roared.

Big Red staggered sideways, regained control of his feet, and lunged straight ahead. I aimed my second shot for his shoulder, and the 240-grain bullet spun him around. He dived into thickets alongside the runway and was gone. I heard him crash through brush; then all was silent. I knew he had fallen.

I went down that tree as fast as I could. I got within 30 yards of him, and then he staggered away. I snapped two shots through the thickets, but the bullets never got to him. I heard him fall again about 60 yards to my right. I got within 40 feet of him before he tried getting up. He couldn’t make it. Another bullet finished him instantly.

I started field-dressing the buck immediately. It wasn’t easy. His bulk was so great I couldn’t move him. I tied his legs to saplings to spread-eagle his hindquarters. Throughout the job, I whistled for Rudy every few minutes. It’s a whistle note we’ve used for woods communication since we were kids. I was nearly done with the chore when Rudy found me. He stayed with the buck while I went to Ross Laster’s farm for help.

Four of the Laster brothers and I got a tractor to within 300 yards of Big Red. Then we had to chop down saplings, clear brush, and cut a fence to get the tractor within 100 yards of the buck. After that it was pure bull work — dragging, hauling, and lifting Big Red till we finally had him balanced on the tractor.

A few hours later, he weighed 260 pounds on a coal scale. I was surprised because I’d figured he would scale over 300 pounds. I guess the massive antlers fooled me. I was familiar with the Boone and Crockett Club method of scoring trophy deer, and I was certain my buck would score near the top of the record list.

Two months later, the antlers scored 185 4/8 points. My trophy won third place for typical whitetails in the Boone and Crockett Club two-year competition period ending December 31, 1965. Though I didn’t kill a new world record, I did score some impressive ratings. Big Red is the best trophy whitetail ever killed in Kentucky.

The inside spread of his rack measures 30 2/8 inches, more than 10 inches wider than the current world record. While checking the last listing of all-time Boone and Crockett records, I discovered that this inside measurement is the greatest among all typical whitetail deer recorded there. Though I realize that total score is all that counts, I doubt whether anyone will ever kill a whitetail buck with a wider antler spread than Big Red’s.

There’s one thing I can guarantee — nobody will ever know a greater hunting thrill than I experienced when I looked over my shoulder in that sycamore and saw the dream of a lifetime coming true.

#8286. A Climbing Expedition to 'Central Asia's Patagonia'

A mix of nine young and veteran Croatian climbers spent the month of August in one of the world’s great big-wall destinations — Kyrgyzstan’s Karavshin Range in the Pamir-Alay Mountains. Reaching up to 5,509m, the once-unknown granite cliffs now draw dozens of international climbers each summer. The two core valleys, Ak-Su and Kara-Su, have become known as Central Asia’s Patagonia.

Deputy leader Lukas Grbac Lackovic spoke to ExplorersWeb about the place and their expedition. First, a summary of their four weeks.

Though suffering from stomach issues for most of the month (more on this later), the team repeated several granite classics, did a new route on 4,430m Pik Breeze, and attempted another new line.

Three climbers — Bruno Crljenic, Eva Pejic, and Lackovic — identified a potential new line below Pik Breeze’s west ridge. They knew of only one previous route on the mountain, done by Russians Marina Popova and Denis Prokofiev.

Beginning at 5am, the three crossed a broad scree slope, then began climbing a couloir below Pik Breeze’s west ridge. They negotiated loose rock, briefly followed an existing line, then moved left into crack systems.

Canned Horse, 6c A0, top. Below, previous attempts and possible other lines on the face.

They climbed until 9pm, when they bivouacked on a tiny ledge with space for only two people sitting and one lying down. Resuming at 8:30am, they reached a col after three pitches and continued directly up slabs and cracks. They finished on easier IV/V terrain and followed a 200m ridge to the summit.

They called their new line Canned Horse, 930m, 23 pitches, 6c A0. It took them a further eight hours to get back to base camp. During the climb, they found pitons on two pitches. They believe these belonged to another route on the west ridge, but the history of that line, and whether it was finished, is uncertain.

Pejic, Grbac Lackovic, and Crljenic on top of Pik Breeze.

Later in the month, one of those climbers, Eva Pejic, became quite ill and couldn’t leave base camp on her own. Five teammates helped evacuate her, carrying her for 11km, with assistance from other climbers in the area. She later recuperated in the Kyrgyz city of Osh.

On the first crux of ‘Perestroika Crack.’

Three small teams of Croatian climbers also repeated Perestroika Crack, one of the best-known long granite routes in Central Asia. It rises about 900m up the north face of 4,240m Pik Slesova and is graded 7a. Three members reportedly free-climbed the route. One pair completed the line in a single marathon day, beginning at 5:45am, summiting at 5:40pm, and returning to base camp at 11pm.

Two of the climbers, Sinisa Skalec and Ivan Vitez, also repeated the French Ridge of 4,510m Kyrkchilta, 2,000m, 6b to 6b+. They needed one bivouac. Toward the end of August, this same pair attempted a first ascent on the Central Pyramid of Ortotyubek, overlooking base camp. Their attempted route mounted slabs and cracks to the left of the established Take It Easy line, which other Croatians had repeated during that month. The pair gave up their attempt on August 26 because of illness.

Base camp with Ortotyubek and Slesova in the background.

Here is our interview with Lukas Grbac Lackovic about Kyrgyzstan and the Ak-Su Valley.

Lukas Grbac Lackovic repeats a route called the Small Russian Tower.

Was Eva Pejic’s health problem related to altitude or something else? What was the illness you experienced on Ortotyubek?

Eva’s health problem was unrelated to altitude exposure or the expedition environment. However, most of us experienced gastrointestinal infections, with symptoms including diarrhea, bloating, fever, and general malaise.

This significantly hindered our climbing progress, as everyone in the team got sick at least once, and some even twice. Recovery was slow and never quite complete –- we felt weak for most of the trip.

One thing that helped us recover was having plain rice with some of our meals, which we could get from the cook if we asked nicely. If we were to go again, we would definitely bring our own food and cooking equipment. This can be inconvenient, but it could potentially save you at least a week of being sick and unable to climb.

Another view of base camp and peaks Ortotyubek and Slesova.

Can you describe the Karavshin Valley? How large is it? Are there many side valleys?

The two main valleys are Ak-Su and Kara-Su. Adjacent to them is the Jaupaya Valley, which provides a descent route from Pik Breeze and is home to several peaks around 5,000m high. The rock quality there appears poor, and we are not aware of any established rock routes in the valley.

Another interesting area, west of Kara Su, is the Orto-Chashma Gorge. An Italian team made a first ascent there during our visit.

Here in the West, we first heard about the area following the kidnapping of four American climbers in Kara-Su in 2000. Since then, it seems to have calmed down and become a popular climbing destination. Is the area considered safe nowadays, or are there still things climbers should be aware of?

Currently, the security situation in the valley is good. There is always the possibility of tensions, of course, as the valleys lie close to the border with Tajikistan. However, in recent years, the number of climbers visiting the area has increased exponentially, reaching around 100 climbers this year.

How many other climbing teams were in Ak-Su and neighboring Kara-Su while you were there? Where were they generally from?

During the three weeks we spent in the valley, up to 50 climbers were in BC at the same time. Climbers came from all over the world — Chile, U.S., Spain, Slovakia, Poland, Belgium, Slovenia, France, Italy, Germany, Japan, Russia…

We had originally planned a different expedition, but had to change our destination just a few months before departure. Some friends from Croatia and Slovenia recommended the area because of its straightforward logistics and relatively good security, while still offering impressive big walls and proper crack climbing. It didn’t take much to convince us!

Are there any military checkpoints? Do you need special permission to enter the valleys?

Yes, you have to pass through a military checkpoint when entering the area. However, the outfitter handles the application for the necessary permits and ensures everything goes smoothly.

Some call the Karavshin Valley the Patagonia of Central Asia because of its aesthetic granite walls. Do you think that’s a fair description?

Patagonia is definitely more spectacular, but you pay the price with poor weather. If your goal is to climb almost every day, then the Karavshin Valley is a better choice.

Climbing in Patagonia requires much more logistical planning and preparation, and the approaches themselves are a whole different story. In the Karavshin Valley, on the other hand, there is no snow or ice during the season we visited (August), at least at the walls we climbed. Some of the walls are just a 15-minute walk from BC, and you can reach them all in approach shoes.

Perestroika Crack and some of the classic routes in the Karavshin region are arguably just as good as the best rock routes in Patagonia.

How does the granite compare to Yosemite and Patagonia?

The granite is more similar in texture to that found in Patagonia; it is not as smooth as in Yosemite. The overall rock quality is generally good, although, as everywhere, some sections are of poorer quality. One downside of the mild climate in Karavshin Valley is the dirt and grass that accumulate in the cracks, which can sometimes detract from the aesthetic appeal of the routes. The more popular and frequently climbed routes have already been cleaned and are pleasant to climb.

You climbed 4-1/2 pitches of the route on Ortotyubek. How much did you have left to complete it?

There were still two-and-a-half pitches left to complete the route up to the junction with Take It Easy. We envisioned the second half of the fifth pitch following the line up to a point just below the overhang that runs diagonally to the left.

From there, the sixth pitch follows a thin crack, from which you need to traverse left and move into another system of thin cracks that runs across the roof and joins the Take It Easy belay (seventh pitch). The last pitch of Take It Easy offers a logical exit, and we don’t think there is any need to come up with an alternative.

At the point where we stopped (first half of the fifth pitch), we left two pitons that we used as a temporary rappel anchor. Repeating parties are welcome to remove them, as they were only left for temporary use. We think a few bolts may be needed in the second half of the fifth pitch, but that obviously depends on the abilities of those planning to complete the route.

All belays are equipped (the first and fourth belays have two 8mm bolts each, while the second and third have two pitons each). In addition, we left two or three pitons in the first pitch and two in the second pitch.

As in the rest of the valley, some sections of the route are filled with dirt and grass. We made an effort to clean the cracks in the first four pitches, but there is still plenty of work to be done, especially on the sixth pitch, which we didn’t climb, where a thin crack is completely filled with dirt.

How much unclimbed rock remains? Are the obvious lines already established, or are there still many promising routes?

The most obvious and accessible lines may have already been climbed, but there is still plenty of potential. Anyone willing to put in the effort can establish a new route. The area is vast, and there is still plenty of room for new routes.

Your website mentions that there are guidebooks to certain routes in that area. Where are these available?

Most of the guidebooks we used are available online. We received some Russian guidebooks from climbing friends, although we didn’t use them very much. We’re not sure how easily they can be found online. Climbers from all over the world bring various materials to the camp, so most route topos and information can be obtained there.

What was the most unexpected experience on your expedition — something that might surprise climbers familiar with other big-wall areas?

We were pleasantly surprised by the kindness and honesty of the Kyrgyz people. When traveling to remote parts of the world, many of us tend to expect that someone will try to rip us off and that we will have to haggle over everything, but that was not the case here.

Although some things took longer than expected, everything we had agreed on in advance was respected, and all the logistics for transportation and accommodation worked very well.

As we mentioned earlier, our only complaint concerns the food and hygiene conditions at the camp, which were most likely responsible for the digestive problems experienced by virtually all the climbers staying there.

Jerry Kobalenko is the editor of ExplorersWeb. One of Canada’s premier arctic travelers, he is the author of The Horizontal Everest and Arctic Eden, and has just finished a book about adventures in Labrador. In 2018, he was awarded the Polar Medal by the Governor General of Canada and in 2022, he received the Queen’s Platinum Jubilee Medal for services to exploration.
